title: Integers versus floats, and why 0.1 plus 0.2 is not 0.3
story:
Add two tenths together in almost any language and the answer has a small tail of unexpected digits on the end. The machine is not broken and the arithmetic is not sloppy. It is doing exactly what it was specified to do.

The representation almost all hardware uses is specified by IEEE 754, first published in 1985, with William Kahan as its principal architect. Its double precision format occupies 64 bits, of which 53 are available for the significand — so a value is stored as a sign, an exponent and a fixed number of significant binary digits.

The consequence follows from the base rather than from the format. In decimal, a third cannot be written finitely: it repeats. In binary, one tenth cannot be written finitely either — it repeats. So the moment a tenth is stored, it is stored as the nearest value the format can express, which is not a tenth. Two of those approximations added together give an approximation of the sum, and the difference becomes visible because the display prints enough digits to show it.

Note what this means for the mental model: the value you wrote in your source code was never in the machine. Every operation afterwards is exact arithmetic on a number slightly different from the one you meant, and the usual shock — that the computer got it wrong — has it backwards. The computer got the conversion right at the moment you wrote the literal, and everything after that is correct arithmetic on a correct approximation.

Rounding error compounds, and the best-documented case is worth telling in full because of what it shows about how such failures actually arrive.

On 25 February 1991 a Patriot battery at Dhahran in Saudi Arabia failed to track and intercept an incoming Scud, which struck an army barracks and killed 28 Americans. The unit had been operating continuously for over 100 hours. Time was kept by the internal clock as an integer count of tenths of a second, and converting it for the prediction arithmetic multiplied it by one tenth in a 24-bit register. One tenth has a non-terminating binary expansion, so it was chopped — and the error grew in proportion to how long the system had been running. After about 100 hours it reached roughly 0.34 seconds. A Scud travels at about 1,676 metres per second, so in that interval it moves more than half a kilometre: far enough to fall outside the range gate being tracked.

Three properties of that failure are worth extracting. It was not random but proportional to uptime, so it was reproducible and invisible on a system that gets restarted. It had no error to report — the software was working, computing the wrong answer confidently. And the magnitude that mattered was not the error itself, which was a third of a second, but the error multiplied by a velocity nobody was thinking about when the conversion was written.

The organisational part is the most uncomfortable and it is in the same report. Israeli data showing a significant range gate shift reached the Patriot Project Office on 11 February. Modified software was released on 16 February. A message on 21 February warned about very long run times without defining a threshold. The corrected software arrived at Dhahran on 26 February — the day after the attack. The fault was known, the fix existed, and the distribution was slower than the events.

What to do about it is short. Do not compare floating point values for equality; compare within a tolerance appropriate to the magnitudes involved. For quantities that must be exact — money above all — store integers of the smallest unit and do the arithmetic there, accepting that you must fix that unit in advance and handle overflow yourself. And be suspicious of any long-running accumulation, because that is the shape the Dhahran failure had: no single operation was wrong, and the total was.

problem.name: Exact in one base, repeating in another
problem.shape: A fractional quantity is stored in binary and then compared or accumulated.
tell: two values that should be equal are not
an error grows with how long a process has run
money is held in a floating point type
a comparison uses exact equality on a computed value
problem.move: Treat a stored float as an approximation with a known bound: compare within a tolerance scaled to the magnitudes involved, and hold anything that must be exact as an integer count of the smallest unit. Examine any long-running accumulation specifically, because that is where a bounded per-operation error becomes an unbounded total.
problem.invariant: A fraction that terminates in decimal need not terminate in binary, so the value written in source is not the value stored — and every subsequent operation is exact arithmetic on a different number.
problem.breaks: Comparing within a tolerance requires choosing one, and a fixed tolerance is wrong at some scale: too tight for large magnitudes, absurdly loose for small ones. So the tolerance has to be relative to the values being compared, which means there is no correct universal answer, only a correct one for a known range.

cost.time: integer arithmetic on the smallest unit requires deciding that unit up front and handling overflow explicitly
cost.space: fixed-point or decimal representations give up the enormous range the exponent provides
cost.beats: using floating point and comparing exactly, which is simplest and intermittently wrong, and using arbitrary-precision decimals everywhere, which is correct and far slower

worked.reasoning:

In decimal a third repeats forever. In binary, one tenth repeats forever. So a tenth is stored as the nearest representable value, which is not a tenth, and adding two such approximations produces an approximation of the sum. The display then prints enough digits to reveal it.

The mental model correction matters more than the mechanism: the number you wrote in source was never in the machine. Every operation afterwards is exact arithmetic on a slightly different number. The usual reaction — the computer got it wrong — is backwards; the conversion was correct at the literal, and everything after is correct arithmetic on a correct approximation.

When it matters is when errors accumulate or when a comparison is exact, and the best-documented case shows both.
